```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(epidemiologysuite)
```

Surveillance asks different questions from a trial: how many people to examine to be fairly sure an infection is absent, how many
to sample to classify an area as above or below a coverage target, and when a weekly count is high enough to call an alarm. The
numbers are computed when this page is built; the examples are those the package's tests check against the published answers or
the reference package (`tests/testthat/test-calc_rule_of_three.R`, `test-calc_lqas.R`, `test-calc_analyze_surveillance.R`). In
the app: **Plan: Sample Size > Surveillance** and **Survey & Cross-Sectional**, and **Analyze > Outbreaks and surveillance**.

## No events seen: the rule of three

If none of n people has the event, the upper 95% confidence limit for its frequency is about 3/n (Hanley & Lippman-Hand 1983).
With 30 people:

```{r r3-bound}
b <- calc_rule_of_three_bound(n = 30, conf_level = 0.95)
c(approximate = round(b$approx_bound, 4), exact = round(b$exact_bound, 4))
```

Turned round: how many people must be seen without an event to be 95% sure that its frequency is below 1%?

```{r r3-n}
r3 <- calc_rule_of_three_n(p = 0.01, conf_level = 0.95)
c(exact = r3$n_exact, rule_of_three = r3$n_approx)
```

## Showing that an infection is absent

How many animals (or people, or farms) to test so that, if the infection were present at a given prevalence, at least one positive
would be found with 95% confidence, allowing for a test that misses some cases. The dairy-herd example of `epiR::epi.ssdetect()`
(Cannon 2001): 1000 animals, a design prevalence of 5%, a test with 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity.

```{r detect}
calc_detect_event_imperfect_test(N = 1000, prev = 0.05, se = 0.90, sp = 1.00, conf_level = 0.95)$n_hypergeometric
```

The function follows epiR 2.0.67; epiR 3.0.0 differs in a few cases, which the help page and the app explain.

## Above or below a target: LQAS

Lot quality assurance sampling classifies an area from a small sample: here coverage of 80% is acceptable and 50% is not, with at
most a 10% chance of each misclassification. The answer is a sample size and a decision rule.

```{r lqas}
lq <- calc_lqas(p_upper = 0.80, p_lower = 0.50, alpha = 0.10, beta = 0.10)
c(sample = lq$n, pass_if_at_least = lq$d)
round(c(alpha = lq$alpha_achieved, beta = lq$beta_achieved), 4)
```

This is the widely used rule of 19 with a decision value of 13.

## Alarms on a weekly count

The EARS methods (C1, C2, C3) compare each week with the weeks just before it; the CUSUM adds up small excesses until they pass a
threshold. A made-up series of 40 weeks of counts around 5, with a rise in the last weeks:

```{r series}
set.seed(1)
counts <- c(rpois(36, 5), 9, 12, 14, 15)
```

```{r ears}
ears <- calc_surveillance_ears(counts, method = "C2")
c(weeks_checked = ears$n_monitored, alarms = ears$n_alarms, first_alarm = ears$first_alarm)
```

```{r cusum}
cu <- calc_surveillance_cusum(counts, type = "poisson", baseline = 14, shift_ratio = 2)
c(weeks_checked = cu$n_monitored, alarms = cu$n_alarms, first_alarm = cu$first_alarm)
```

`first_alarm` is the week of the series in which the method first signals. The rise starts in week 37, so any alarm before it is a
false one: here C2 first signals in week `r ears$first_alarm` and the CUSUM in week `r cu$first_alarm`. The threshold sets the
trade-off between false alarms in quiet weeks and a late signal in a real outbreak: lower it and alarms come earlier, but more often
for nothing.

## Outbreak investigation

Attack rates, a food-specific attack-rate table, secondary attack rates and the case fatality rate, from counts you already have:
`calc_analyze_attack_rate()`, `calc_analyze_exposure_table()`, `calc_analyze_secondary_attack()`, `calc_analyze_case_fatality()`.

Each help page gives the source of its formula and an example.
